Two different statistical paradigms




Until Last Week

Statistical Estimation & Modeling Goal: Explain mechanisms & test hypotheses. Inference, parameters, confidence intervals, and interpretability.



This Week

Statistical Learning & Prediction Goal: Predict outcome on unseen data. Focuses on generalization and predictive accuracy, often trading off interpretability.




Statistical Learning splits into two primary paradigms:

Structure Discovery Analyze features (\(X\)) without target labels (\(Y\)). How many useful dimensions? Are samples similar? Are there clusters?

PCAUMAPClustering

Principal component analysis · unsupervised



InputsA table of standardized metabolite intensities.


Orthogonal directionsPC1 captures the greatest remaining variance; PC2 is orthogonal and captures the next greatest.

title: Statistics for Pharmacists
section: PCA is blind to disease labels
text:
PCA is blind to disease labels

Variance ≠ class separation



Wrong objective“Choose the 2D view with the greatest separation between sick and healthy patients” is not PCA’s optimization goal.


Correct objectiveChoose orthogonal directions with maximal retained data variance.


Possible consequenceClass separation can emerge—but it can also hide in a low-variance direction.




Principal components are linear combinations of original variables and might not be interpretable, e.g. \(\mathrm{PC_1} = 0.316 \, \mathrm{weight} + 0.947 \, \mathrm{hemoglobin} - 0.053 \, \mathrm{age}\), and keep in mind the original variables have already been z-score scaled.

From compressed data to discovered groups

Unsupervised clustering



InputData with no known class labels.


AlgorithmDefines a notion of same-group membership.


OutputAn assigned partition or cluster probabilities—not verified clinical diagnoses.




Look at 3 algorithms.


K-means assumes compact groups: minimizes within-cluster squared Euclidean distances from centroids.


Gaussian mixture is a probability model: estimates mean, covariance and mixture weight for each component.

Memorization versus generalization

The central machine-learning problem






A flexible model can fit all observed points while performing poorly on new measurements. Training error alone cannot detect that.

High bias · low flexibilityMisses the real trend: underfitting.


High variance · high flexibilityLearns specific sample fluctuations: overfitting.


Lower future riskAppropriate complexity, representative data and regularization.

section: Prevalence: how many are affected now?
text:
Prevalence: how many are affected now?

Disease burden · stock of existing cases


\(\mathrm{Prevalence}=\dfrac{\text{existing cases}}{\text{population at time / period}}\)




Illustrative population


1,000 people


Observed at the start of the year




Already affected


50 people


Point prevalence = 50 / 1,000 = 5%





Prevalence describes population burden. It reflects both arrival of new cases and how long people remain cases.

title: Statistics for Pharmacists
text:
Incidence: how many become affected?

New events among people initially at risk





\(\text{Cumulative incidence}=40/950\approx4.2\%\) during 1 year



Cumulative incidence is a risk over a specified time horizon, assuming appropriate follow-up and accounting for censoring when needed.

title: Statistics for Pharmacists
text:
Incidence rate uses person-time

A different denominator and unit


\(\text{Incidence rate}=\dfrac{\text{new cases}}{\sum\text{person-time at risk}}\)




Example


40 new cases


Among a dynamic followed population




Observed time


900 person-years


Different people contribute different durations




Incidence rate


4.44 / 100 person-years


An event rate, not a 4.44% probability




Rate and probability become close only under additional conditions, including relatively low risk over the time horizon.

title: Statistics for Pharmacists
text:
Confounder or effect modifier?

Two different scientific questions



Concept


What happens?


What should we do?


Confounding


An overall estimate is distorted by differing group compositions


Adjustment aims at an association net of the confounding pathway


Effect modification


Exposure–outcome associations genuinely differ between strata


Report the strata; an overall effect can conceal clinically useful differences




Our synthetic drink example illustrates both:


\(RR\) within low rent \(= 2.0\);


\(RR\) within high rent \(= 1.33\);


pooled \(RR = 1.0\).

Drug response across three hospitals





Drug: 30%, 60%, 90% success in hospitals A/B/C; control: 20%, 50%, 80%. Different arm allocations create the pooled reversal.

title: Statistics for Pharmacists
text:
When the confounder is measured

Design and analysis options



01Before data collectionRestriction or matching can improve comparability; randomization addresses baseline confounding by design.


02During analysisStratify, standardize or adjust using regression; always inspect effect modification.


03If effects are broadly commonMantel–Haenszel estimates an adjusted association across strata (with a clear target estimand).




A common pooled effect is not appropriate when stratum-specific treatment effects differ substantially.

What if confounding is unobserved?

A fundamental limit of observational evidence




Propensity methods


Measured covariates


Matching / weighting / adjustment can balance observed confounders




Sensitivity analysis


Unmeasured covariates


Ask how strong hidden confounding must be to reverse a result




Triangulate


Different designs


Compare evidence across designs with different weaknesses





These approaches do not automatically solve unmeasured confounding; more sophisticated methods are outside this course.

From Mass Action to the Boltzmann Sigmoid

First-principles derivation · Binding kinetics & cooperativity





1: Equilibrium Mass Action


Receptor \(\text{R}\) binds ligand \(\text{L}\): \[\text{L} + \text{R} \underset{k_{\mathrm{off}}}{\overset{k_{\mathrm{on}}}{\rightleftharpoons}} \text{RL}, \quad K_{\mathrm{d}} = \frac{[\text{L}][\text{R}]}{[\text{RL}]}\]


\[\theta = \frac{[\text{RL}]}{[\text{R}]_{\mathrm{tot}}} = \frac{[\text{L}]}{[\text{L}] + K_{\mathrm{d}}}\]


Hyperbolic response curve on a linear concentration scale (\([\text{L}]\)).





2: Log-Dose reparameterization


Define log-concentration \(x = \log[\text{L}]\) and log-dissociation \(x_{50} = \log K_{\mathrm{d}}\):


\[\theta = \frac{e^x}{e^x + e^{x_{50}}} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(x - x_{50})}}\]


This is exactly the standard logistic (Boltzmann) sigmoid on the log-dose axis.





3: Hill Cooperativity (\(n_{\mathrm{H}}\))


Multi-site binding (\(n_{\mathrm{H}}\) molecules bind cooperatively):


\[\theta = \frac{[\text{L}]^{n_{\mathrm{H}}}}{[\text{L}]^{n_{\mathrm{H}}} + K_{\mathrm{d}}^{n_{\mathrm{H}}}} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-n_{\mathrm{H}}(x - x_{50})}}\]


The Hill coefficient \(n_{\mathrm{H}}\) directly scales the slope factor (steepness) of the sigmoid.




Mechanistic insight: The logistic curve is not just an empirical smoothing function—it arises naturally when ligand-receptor equilibrium is plotted against log-concentration. \(n_{\mathrm{H}} > 1\) indicates positive cooperativity, while \(n_{\mathrm{H}} < 1\) reflects negative cooperativity or multiple receptor subtypes.

\[\hat y = 0.050 + 0.075x, \quad A_{\mathrm{obs}} = 0.650\]

Assigned Uncertainties:• Measurement error (known from measuring triplicate): \(\mathrm{SE}_{Abs} = 0.003\)• Intercept error (known from calibration): \(\mathrm{SE}_{\beta_0} = 0.040\)• Slope error (known from calibration): \(\mathrm{SE}_{\beta_1} = 0.002\)





2: Delta Method (Propagation of Uncertainty)


\[\mathrm{SE}(\hat x) \approx \sqrt{ \left(\tfrac{\partial \hat x}{\partial Abs}\right)^2\!\mathrm{SE}_{Abs}^2 + \left(\tfrac{\partial \hat x}{\partial \beta_0}\right)^2\!\mathrm{SE}_{\beta_0}^2 + \left(\tfrac{\partial \hat x}{\partial \beta_1}\right)^2\!\mathrm{SE}_{\beta_1}^2 }\]




• Assay (\(Abs\)): \(\left(\frac{1}{0.075} \cdot 0.003\right)^2 = 0.040^2 = \mathbf{0.0016}\)


• Intercept (\(\beta_0\)): \(\left(-\frac{1}{0.075} \cdot 0.040\right)^2 = (-0.533)^2 = \mathbf{0.2844}\)


• Slope (\(\beta_1\)): \(\left(-\frac{8.0}{0.075} \cdot 0.002\right)^2 = (-0.213)^2 = \mathbf{0.0455}\)



\[\mathrm{SE}(\hat x) = \sqrt{0.0016 + 0.2844 + 0.0455} \approx \mathbf{0.576\text{ mg/L}}\]


Approx. 95% CI: \(8.0 \pm 1.15\text{ mg/L}\) (\(6.85 \text{ to } 9.15\text{ mg/L}\))




Key Takeaway: The calibration parameters (\(\beta_0, \beta_1\)) account for over \(99.5\%\) of total variance (\(0.3299\text{ (mg/L)}^2\)), while the single-measurement assay noise (\(Abs\)) contributes less than \(0.5\%\) (\(0.0016\text{ (mg/L)}^2\)).

section: Transformation is not a free fix
text:
Transformation is not a free fix


Exponential\(y=a\,e^{b\,x}\) transforms to \(\log y=\log a+b\,x\) for \(y>0\), but error remains multiplicative on original scale.


Power / allometry\(y=a\,x^b\) transforms to \(\log y=\log a+b\,\log x\) for \(x,y>0\), but error remains multiplicative on original scale.


Inverse / hyperbolic\(y=\frac{a\,x}{b+x}\) transforms to \(\frac{1}{y}=\frac{1}{a}+\frac{b}{a}\,\frac{1}{x}\) but reciprocal transformation amplifies noise at low \(x\).


Logarithmic\(y=a+b\,\log x\) would transform to \(e^y=e^a\,x^b\), but we can just fit \(y\) versus \(\log x\) for \(x>0\).



Changing the scale changes the error model and what squared deviations mean. Direct nonlinear fitting is often preferable to transforming noisy response data.


Further generalizing the above relationships renders linear transformation impossible altogether. For example \(y=a\,e^{b\,(x-c)}+d\), where \(d\) represents a constant shift in the response and \(c\) a time lag in the measurement.

Chemistry or physiology motivates the equation, not just convenient flexibility.

Iterative algorithms may converge slowly, fail, or reach a local solution.

Nonlinear regression can still minimize an SSE; what becomes nonlinear is the dependence of predictions on unknown parameters.


How do iterations move from starting values? Unlike linear regression—where linear algebra takes us straight to the exact global solution in one step (or via Dantzig’s simplex algorithm in linear programming)—nonlinear models require iterative optimization algorithms.


Gradient-guided vs. derivative-free search: Algorithms like the Damped Gauss-Newton (seen in our widget) or Levenberg-Marquardt use local gradient and curvature directions as a guide to nudge parameters toward lower SSE. When gradients cannot be calculated, derivative-free algorithms (e.g., Nelder-Mead, grid/random search, or evolutionary algorithms) explore the parameter space instead—an entire optimization discipline beyond our scope.

Automatic camera inspection

A distribution describes how probability is spread across possible outcomes.

Discrete random variable


Possible values are separated. Individual values can have positive probability.

Continuous random variable


Possible values fill an interval. Probability belongs to ranges, not exact points.







Random number: \(X\in[0,1]\)



  





Discrete probability lives on values. Continuous probability lives over intervals.



Use a fair die rather than a coin as the flagship discrete-uniform example. Reserve the coin for Bernoulli.

Binary and finite equal-chance mechanisms




Degenerate


The outcome is fixed.


\(\mathbb{P}(X=c)=1\)





Discrete uniform


Finite outcomes equally likely.


\(\mathbb{P}(X=x)=1/k\)

k = 6

One yes/no experiment.

Successes in \(n\) independent Bernoulli trials.

n = 6   p = 0.50

Count events in a fixed exposure interval.


\(\mathbb{P}(X=k)=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}\)

When bad statistics has consequences

Case study · Sally Clark


A figure presented in court for the probability of a sudden infant death in a family like Clark’s was approximately

\[P(\text{one SIDS death}) \approx \frac{1}{8543}\]


The probability of two deaths was then presented by multiplying the number by itself:

\[\frac{1}{8543}\times\frac{1}{8543}\approx\frac{1}{73\,000\,000}\]





What assumption is hiding inside that multiplication?




Do not solve this yet — we return to it after independence.



This is deliberately unresolved. The case will return after the independence slide later in Week 1.
Avoid turning this into a legal-history digression. The statistical point is that multiplication of probabilities encodes assumptions.

Independence is a scientific assumption

When learning B tells us nothing about A




Independent


\(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)=\mathbb{P}(A)\)

Knowing \(B\) does not change the probability of \(A\).




Dependent


Adverse effectandrenal impairment

Multiplication of unconditional probabilities is only justified after the independence assumption is justified.



This is a major conceptual slide. Make students say the scientific assumption aloud: are these events independent in the real world?

The hidden assumption


\[
\frac{1}{8543}\times\frac{1}{8543}
\]



This multiplication assumes independence.





Siblings may share genetic and environmental risk factors.


The calculation also confused:

\[\mathbb{P}(\text{evidence} \mid \text{hypothesis})\]

with:

\[\mathbb{P}(\text{hypothesis} \mid \text{evidence})\]






Independence is not a default setting. It is a claim about how the world works.



This is the payoff from the earlier unresolved mystery. Do not spend long on legal details.
Say clearly: even if a probability number is correct in one context, combining it with another probability can become invalid when assumptions are unjustified.

Not the same question.

The formula compresses the counting logic


\[
\mathbb{P}(D\mid +)=\frac{\mathbb{P}(+\mid D)\cdot \mathbb{P}(D)}{\mathbb{P}(+)}
\]


\[

Bayes’ theorem is a mathematical model for updating probabilities when new evidence arrives.



Avoid saying Bayes is the entire foundation of the scientific method. Say it formalizes an important type of evidence updating.
Connect it to the learning loop: prior state of knowledge → new data → updated state of knowledge.

\(\displaystyle n^k\)

Probability is a mathematical language for uncertainty.


\(\mathbb{P}(A\mid B)\neq \mathbb{P}(B\mid A)\)

patients with hypersensitivity




?

Parameter?

Best guess?

Likelihood is not the probability that the parameter is true. It is a compatibility score for parameter values given the observed data.

How data are generated


We now see how reliable data generating processes are.

Study-design tree

Was exposure or treatment assigned by the investigator?






Study design





Observational


researcher observes exposure/outcome as they occur




Experimental


researcher assigns intervention or condition





Descriptive


describe frequency, distribution, case patterns




Analytical observational


cross-sectional · cohort · case-control




Clinical / interventional


control, randomization, blinding, endpoint definition





Design goal


make comparisons interpretable





The key first branch is assignment. If the investigator assigns exposure/treatment, it is experimental. Otherwise it is observational, even if the analysis is complex.

title: Statistics for Pharmacists
text:
Three observational directions

For analytical observations: Direction of observation matters




Cross-sectional


measure exposure and outcome at one snapshot


exposure ↔︎ outcome




Cohort


classify by exposure, then follow outcomes


exposure → outcome




Case-control


start from outcome status, look backward for exposure


outcome → exposure history







Keep the examples pharmaceutical: drug exposure and adverse event; smoking and lung disease; genotype and hypersensitivity.

Experimental studies assign intervention

For clinical trials: Assignment is the defining move




Eligible patients


defined inclusion/exclusion criteria



→



Treatment assignment


ideally randomized



→



Endpoint measurement


predefined outcome





Clinical experiments try to make treatment groups comparable except for the intervention.



Do not yet dive into p-values. The point is that experimental design creates the conditions under which a comparison may support causal interpretation.

title: Statistics for Pharmacists
text:
Parallel and crossover trials

Two common clinical structures




Parallel design


randomize→Drug A→outcome


randomize→Drug B→outcome




Crossover design


Drug A→washout→Drug B


Drug B→washout→Drug A





Crossover studies can be efficient, but require attention to carryover and washout.



Mention that crossover is not suitable when disease changes rapidly, treatment has lasting effects, or cure/outcome cannot be reset.

title: Statistics for Pharmacists
text:
Clinical trial design levers

Small design choices can change interpretation




Comparator


placebo, standard therapy, dose group, active control




Randomization


protects against systematic allocation differences




Blinding


reduces expectation and observation effects




Endpoint


must be clinically meaningful and measurable





The data are only as interpretable as the comparison the design created.



Mention double-dummy designs verbally: used when interventions look different, such as tablet versus injection, to preserve blinding.

title: Statistics for Pharmacists
text:
Evidence depends on the question

A cautious hierarchy for causal treatment questions




Descriptive


what appears to be happening?



→



Observational analytical


associations under real-world conditions



→



Randomized comparative experiment


stronger protection against confounding





∑


Meta-analysis & Systematic Review Synthesizes and pools evidence across available and eligible studies




Stronger design does not automatically mean better evidence: execution, relevance, measurement quality and bias still matter.



Avoid teaching a rigid evidence pyramid. The best evidence depends on the question: efficacy, safety, rare adverse events, mechanism, diagnostic performance, or real-world utilization.

title: Statistics for Pharmacists
text:
Correlation is not causation

A hidden common cause can structure the comparison


                

Disease severity


Drug choice


Outcome




If sicker patients are more likely to receive the strongest drug, crude outcomes can confuse treatment effect with baseline risk.



Use the phrase confounding by indication: the reason a patient receives a treatment is itself related to prognosis.

title: Statistics for Pharmacists
text:
Why randomization helps

Not magic, but a powerful design principle




Without randomization


clinician choice, patient preference, disease severity and access can all influence treatment group membership




With randomization


treatment assignment is independent of baseline characteristics in expectation





\[
\text{randomization} \;
\not\Rightarrow\; \text{identical groups}
\]




Randomization protects against systematic confounding; chance imbalance can still occur.



This corrects the common misconception that randomization guarantees balanced groups in a particular trial. It balances on average over repeated randomizations.

title: Statistics for Pharmacists
text:
Observational causal reasoning

Bradford Hill considerations help structure judgment




Temporality


cause precedes effect




Dose-response


stronger exposure, stronger effect?




Plausibility


compatible with biological mechanism?




Consistency


seen across settings and methods?





These are considerations, not a checklist that proves causality.



Mention confounding control as an analytic requirement: stratification, matching, regression adjustment, propensity scores later if relevant. Keep this introductory.

Stratification can reveal the hidden structure

Simpson’s paradox: Compare like with like



Treatment


Lower-risk


Higher-risk


Overall


Drug A success rate

273/350 = 78%

234/270 = 87%

Within both risk strata, A looks better. In the aggregate, B looks better.

Aggregation can hide the variable that structures the comparison.

Accuracy × precision

Four measurement patterns




low bias · low variance

high bias · high variance








Beyond Bias & Variance: Key Related Measurement Concepts






🎯

Agreement & Alignment




Association: Asks if measurements are informative about a benchmark. A perfect monotonic relationship can exist even with massive systematic bias.


Consensus / Concordance: Asks if two datasets coincide directly (either exactly or within tolerance)—i.e., whether overall total error is low.


Interchangeability: Asks if measurement differences are small enough that two quantitative methods can replace one another in practice.






🔄

The “R” Metrics (Variability-Focused)




These address variability under varying conditions—saying nothing about bias.



Reliability / Repeatability: Same operator, same instrument, same objects under identical conditions.


Replicability & Reproducibility: Relaxes strict constraints by introducing different objects or operators.


Robustness: Resistance when a justifiably similar but distinct method/instrument is used.


Ruggedness: Resistance of measurement precision to minor, unguided environmental fluctuations.






Use the target as a visual metaphor. The orange crosshair is truth/target. Blue dots are repeated measurements. Students usually grasp accuracy/precision quickly through this image.

Smoothing: what should survive?


SignalStructured variation relevant to the scientific question.


NoiseVariation we hope to attenuate, which may itself contain meaningful events.


Trade-offAggressive smoothing erases sharp peaks and can bias maxima or event timing.




Choose a smoother with the scientific endpoint in mind, not only how pleasing the final curve looks.

title: Statistics for Pharmacists
text:
Moving average



\(\widehat y_t=\dfrac{1}{2k+1}\sum_{j=-k}^{k}y_{t+j}\)



Window widthA wider window attenuates short-term fluctuation.


CostSharp peaks flatten; edge values need special handling.



A simple local average is not a regression model for the underlying mechanism.

title: Statistics for Pharmacists
text:
Savitzky–Golay / LOESS: local polynomial fitting




Within each windowFit a low-degree polynomial to nearby observed points.


At the window centerUse the fitted central value; then slide the window.


In practiceRetains local peaks and derivatives better than a boxcar average in many settings.




Polynomial degree must be smaller than the odd window length; excessive degree may overfit noise.

section: A different time question: time until an event
text:
A different time question: time until an event


EventDeath, relapse, adverse effect, or another defined endpoint.


Start timeDiagnosis, first dose, randomization or enrollment.


ComplicationSome people have not had an event by their last known follow-up.




Survival analysis is about time to event, not necessarily death.

title: Statistics for Pharmacists
text:
Censoring differs from truncation


Mechanism


What is known?


Right censor


Event time exceeds the final observation time. We only know the event time is greater than the last known check.


Left censor


Event happened before the first reliable observation.


Interval censor


Event happened in between two inspection or check-in times, rather than at a precise timestamp.


Left truncation


Observations below a certain threshold are left out of the sample.


Right truncation


Observations above a certain threshold are excluded from the dataset.



Censoring is partial information: the subject is included in the study, but the exact time of the event is unknown; we only know that the event happened within a certain range or relative to a specific point.


With truncation, data points outside a specific range are completely excluded from the dataset; if an observation is truncated, we do not even know it exists.

\(d_i\)Number with the event at that time.

Right censoring reduces subsequent risk sets but does not itself cause a drop in the KM curve.

Visual evidenceStep heights and separation suggest differences in event timing.


InferenceA log-rank test or Cox model addresses a defined comparison.


LimitationsCensoring, competing events and non-proportional hazards matter.




Median survival is the first time at which estimated \(S(t)\) reaches or falls below \(0.5\); it may be unreached.

title: Statistics for Pharmacists
section: Hazard: the danger conditional on survival
text:
Hazard: the danger conditional on survival

\(h(t)=\lim_{\Delta t\to0}\dfrac{\mathbb{P}(t\le T<t+\Delta t\mid T\ge t)}{\Delta t}\)



Survival\(S(t)\): Probability event time is later than \(t\).


CDF\(1-S(t)\): Probability the event has occurred by \(t\).


Hazard\(h(t)\): An instantaneous conditional event rate (probability density), not a probability.




Intuition: While the survival function tells us the probability of making it past a certain point, the hazard function tells us how intense the danger is at that moment, given that we have survived up to that moment.

section: Hazard can rise, fall, or stay constant
text:

Illustrative mechanisms: wear-out, early vulnerability, and memoryless exponential survival.

section: The area under survival measures time
text:
The area under survival measures time

\(E[T]=\int_0^\infty S(t)\,dt\)



Mean or expected survival time is life expectancy.


With incomplete follow-up, restricted mean survival time (RMST) integrates only to a prespecified horizon \(\tau\).




SurvivalHow much of the population remains event-free?


HazardHow intense is the instantaneous event rate?

section: Cox regression keeps baseline hazard flexible
text:
Cox regression keeps baseline hazard flexible

\(h(t\mid x)=h_0(t)\exp(\beta_1x_1+\cdots+\beta_px_p)\)



Baseline hazardTime-changing hazard at the reference covariate profile.


Exponential multiplierCovariates multiply the instantaneous hazard.


Primary assumptionCovariate hazard ratios are constant over time in a proportional-hazards model.






David Cox

title: Statistics for Pharmacists
section: Same changing baseline; different hazard multipliers
text:
Same changing baseline; different hazard multipliers




Hazard ratio 1.8 means 80% higher instantaneous hazard (at a given time), not 80% higher probability of an event.



Baseline hazard \(h_0(t)\): general instantaneous hazard, applies to reference covariate profile


Hazard ratio \(e^{\beta_i}\): \(+1\) unit increase in \(x_i\) multiplies baseline hazard by this much.


Proportional hazards assumption: if smoking increase instantaneous hazard by 2× at 40 years of age, it must also increase it by 2× at 60 years of age. The absolute amount of danger may change over time if baseline hazard changes, but the relative difference between the groups is locked in parallel.

title: Statistics for Pharmacists
text:
What if proportional hazards fails?


CheckCurves and diagnostics may suggest time-varying effects.


AlternativesTime-varying coefficients, stratified Cox, or accelerated failure-time models.


ScopeThese are honorable mentions; learn the interpretation of HR and KM first.
